title: What is an LBO?
subtitle: Leveraged Buyout - buying a company using debt leverage
openingQuestion: A Private Equity fund buys a company worth 1,000 billion using 200 billion of its own capital plus 800 billion in debt. What is this?
openingOptions: An LBO - Leveraged Buyout: buying with a large amount of debt leverage
explanation: A leveraged buyout uses a large amount of debt to buy a company, then uses that company's own cash flow to pay the debt down over time. Profit for the fund comes from three sources: debt shrinking makes the equity slice thicker, operating profit improving, and selling at a higher multiple than the purchase price. Because the debt obligation is fixed, a suitable target needs stable cash flow and low capital spending needs.

diagram.label: The PE fund buys the company with 60-80% debt
The company's cash flow gradually pays down the debt
Equity value multiplies thanks to leverage

realWorldExample.description: KKR's $25 billion LBO of RJR Nabisco is one of the largest and most famous LBO deals in history - becoming the symbol of the leveraged buyout wave of the 1980s, chronicled in the classic book "Barbarians at the Gate".

quiz.question: What is the most important characteristic of an LBO target company?
options: Revenue growth above thirty percent
Stable, predictable free cash flow
A large market capitalization with good stock liquidity
A young leadership team full of product innovation
quiz.explanation: LBOs need: high and stable FCF (to pay interest and principal), real assets as collateral, low revenue volatility, a management team that can be retained. A high-growth tech company with low FCF is usually unsuitable.

quiz.question: Why do Private Equity funds doing LBOs especially favor companies with stable, predictable cash flow (like essential consumer goods) over high-growth but uncertain companies (like early-stage tech)?
options: Because the consumer sector faces much less regulatory intervention than banking
Because high-growth companies are usually too expensive to buy
Because the debt must be repaid on schedule no matter how the business performs
Because stable cash flow helps the business be resold faster
quiz.explanation: Because LBOs use enormous debt leverage, the ability to repay debt on schedule is a make-or-break factor of the deal structure - stable, predictable cash flow (not high growth) is what matters most when weighing an LBO target.

quiz.question: Buying a company for 1,000 billion, 70% debt. Selling it later for 1,300 billion after paying off the principal. What is the return on equity?
options: Equity doesn't change because the gain belongs to the lenders
Equity of 300 billion becomes 390 billion, a gain of exactly 30%
Equity of 700 billion becomes 1,000 billion, a gain of about 43%
Equity of 300 billion becomes 600 billion, doubling
quiz.explanation: Starting equity was 300 billion. Selling for 1,300 billion, paying off 700 billion in debt, leaves 600 billion. The company's enterprise value only rose 30%, but equity doubled - that is leverage's entire mechanism, and it runs exactly as fiercely in reverse when the sale price falls.

quiz.question: What are the three sources of profit in an LBO deal?
options: Paying down debt, improving operations, and a higher exit multiple
Cutting dividends, raising the selling price, and reducing tax owed
Issuing more shares, buying a competitor, and listing early
Selling off assets, laying off staff, and moving headquarters overseas
quiz.explanation: Using cash flow to pay down debt grows the equity slice over time; improving EBITDA grows the whole pie; selling at a higher multiple than at purchase. The third source depends on the market, so it's the one a PE fund controls least.

quiz.question: What is the biggest risk of an LBO structure?
options: The old leadership refuses to stay on after the deal officially closes
Cash flow falls short of forecast while interest still must be paid
The PE fund can't find a buyer after exactly five years
Regulators require cutting the debt ratio below 50%
quiz.explanation: Leverage turns one bad year of business into a liquidity crisis. A company without debt simply earns a bit less; a company inside an LBO can breach its covenants and lose the business outright to its lenders.

keyTakeaways: LBO: buying a company with 60-80% debt
Debt is repaid from the target company's own FCF
PE target: IRR of 20-30%+ over 5-7 years

practicePrompt.question: A private equity (PE) fund buys a company worth 1,000 billion, but puts up only 250 billion of the fund's own cash, with the remaining 750 billion borrowed and secured against the target company's own assets/cash flow. What kind of transaction is this an example of?
options: LBO (Leveraged Buyout): 75% of the purchase price is debt, secured by the company itself
This is an example of an IPO, because the company is moving from private to public
This is an example of Venture Capital, because the fund is making a risky investment in a company
This is an example of a buyback, because the company is repurchasing its own shares
practicePrompt.explanation: LBO: buying a company with 60-80% debt (here, 75%). This high-leverage structure helps the PE fund amplify its return on invested capital if the deal succeeds, but also significantly increases the financial risk for the target company, which must now carry a large debt load.

summary.keyIdea: LBO: buying a company with 60-80% debt
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: Debt is repaid from the target company's own FCF

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: Look up a famous LBO deal (domestic or international) you've heard of in the news, and try to determine: did the target company have stable enough cash flow to service the acquisition debt?
application.secondary: Understanding LBO logic helps you explain why some acquisitions use so much debt.

sections.text: An LBO (Leveraged Buyout) is the signature strategy of Private Equity funds: buy a company mostly with borrowed money, then use that target company's own cash flow to pay the debt down gradually, betting that equity value will multiply thanks to leverage by the time of exit.

In an LBO, a PE fund buys a company with 60-80% of the value coming from debt, with the rest being the fund's own equity. The debt is paid down gradually over the 5-7 year holding period, mainly from the free cash flow (FCF) the target company generates. At exit, if the company's enterprise value has risen, the equity value the PE fund holds multiplies thanks to the leverage effect - because debt has been paid down while the company's value has risen. PE funds typically target an IRR (internal rate of return) of 20-30%+ for LBO deals.
Why LBOs only suit certain types of companies

Because the LBO structure uses very large debt leverage, the target company needs stable, predictable operating cash flow to ensure it has enough cash to pay the interest and principal on its enormous debt on time every year - a company with uncertain cash flow would be very risky in this structure. That's why the ideal characteristics of an LBO target are: high and stable FCF, real assets as collateral, low revenue volatility, and low CapEx. A high-growth tech company with low FCF is usually unsuitable for an LBO, while essential consumer goods companies are a favored target.

items: LBO: buying a company with 60-80% of the capital coming from debt
Debt is paid down gradually from the target company's own free cash flow, not from the PE fund
Characteristics that suit an LBO target: stable cash flow, good collateral assets, low revenue volatility
Historical example: RJR Nabisco (1989, $25 billion) - the iconic LBO deal, chronicled in 'Barbarians at the Gate'

lines: An LBO doesn't create value out of thin air - it amplifies whatever value (or risk) is already present in the target company's cash flow.
